outcome: Makki Naciri (2025, in Integers) proved that if x±1 is 7-free, then n = 4, 5, 7 are the only solutions of the exact equation n!+1=x^2, and more generally that the equation has only finitely many solutions whenever x±1 is k-free (k≥2) or a prime power — the strongest unconditional restricted result yet on the classical equation; the general conjecture remains open.
summary: Brocard's problem — whether n!+1=m^2 has solutions other than n=4,5,7 — remains open in general as of September 2026. The most substantial genuine progress in the window is Abderrahim Makki Naciri's paper 'On the Brocard-Ramanujan Equation with 7-Free Integers and Prime Powers' (Zenodo/arXiv preprint dated 2025-08-15, published in Integers, Vol. 25 (2025), and independently confirmed as the current best-known result by the erdosproblems.com database entry for this problem). Naciri proves that the classical equation n!+1=x^2 has only finitely many solutions when x±1 is k-free (k≥2) or a prime power, and specifically that if x±1 is 7-free, n=4,5,7 are the only solutions. This is a genuine restriction of the exact stated equation (a case, not a variant, since it constrains the same unknowns in the same equation rather than changing the equation), so it counts as `partial` with `resolution_direction` confirmed (the restricted case matches Erdős's conjectured answer). I could not access the full text of Naciri's paper (only the Zenodo/erdosproblems summaries), so I cannot directly quote methodology, but nothing in any secondary source suggests computer-algebra or AI assistance; this is standard analytic/algebraic number theory. Separately, a 2026 arXiv paper by Eric F. Bravo, 'On Brocard's problem with Padovan and Perrin numbers' (arXiv:2606.28577, submitted 2026-06-26), proves (n,x)=(4,5) is the only solution when x is restricted to being a term of the Padovan or Perrin sequence — also a genuine restricted case of the same equation, though narrower in scope than Naciri's result and not the basis for the status here since it postdates and is subsumed in spirit by the stronger, peer-reviewed Naciri result. A separate and unrelated development is Wataru Takeda's complete resolution of the *polynomial analogue* of the Brocard-Ramanujan problem (over F_q[T], published in Finite Fields and Their Applications, online 2025-09-30, print Feb 2026) — this changes the problem (integers to polynomial rings) rather than restricting it, so per §3.1 it is a related problem, not a case, and does not affect the status of the integer problem, which its own announcement explicitly states remains unsolved. A 2024 paper, 'Solution of Brocard's Problem' by Mohamed Imteaz Karimullah (Indian Journal of Advanced Mathematics, Vol. 4 Issue 1, April 2024, an APC-funded journal from Lattice Science Publication with no evidence of MathSciNet/zbMATH indexing or expert digestion, and whose claimed full resolution of a 150-year-old open problem in a minor journal without any subsequent citation, media coverage, or expert acknowledgement is a strong red flag), claims to prove there are no other solutions; I could not extract readable text from its PDF and found no independent verification, citation, or discussion of it anywhere (not on Wikipedia, not on erdosproblems.com, not in any survey). Given the complete absence of expert corroboration and the journal's profile, I do not treat this claim as a `claimed` or `resolved` event — it does not meet even the `claimed` bar of a credible, digestible preprint, and including it would overstate what happened. No AI involvement was found anywhere in the search: no lab announcement, no paper crediting a language model or other AI system with proving, assisting, or bounding any part of this problem. All identified work is conventional human mathematics in refereed or preprint venues.
competing_reading: One could argue the Karimullah (2024) IJAM paper should be recorded as a `claimed` resolution event since it explicitly asserts a full proof of the classical conjecture within the window. I did not adopt this reading because `claimed` requires a credible preprint or machine-checked certificate that experts simply haven't gotten to yet, and this paper shows none of the hallmarks of a serious attempt reaching that bar (no citations, no engagement from the number theory community, publication venue with pay-to-publish characteristics, and its claim would be one of the most significant results in elementary number theory in decades if genuine). Also arguable: whether the Bravo (Padovan/Perrin) 2026 paper should be cited as an additional supporting `partial` event alongside Naciri's — I mention it in summary but treat Naciri's as the decisive event since it is peer-reviewed, more general, and already independently verified by erdosproblems.com.
what_would_settle_it: Reading the full text of the Karimullah (2024) paper's proof (I could only fetch raw PDF bytes, not rendered text) and checking whether it has since been cited, refuted, or corrected in the literature would resolve whether it merits inclusion as a claimed event. Reading Naciri's full paper in Integers would let me quote its methods directly rather than relying on the erdosproblems.com and Zenodo summaries.

judgement.doubts: Naciri's restriction is on the solution x (x±1 7-free), a genuine case of the stated equation. Only the Zenodo page and erdosproblems.com summary were read, not the Integers paper; Integers publication taken from the record. Takeda's date is the online publication date, the first preprint date is not in the record. Karimullah set aside as not_credible, though the record could not read its PDF.
